item.title: The Power of Small Words
item.description:
Resilience

The Power of Small Words

The words that change lives rarely come from Plato. They're from small moments.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • The words that change lives are rarely famous; they are small, personal, and perfectly timed.
  • A single word can reawaken memory, attachment, and a reason to stay.
  • Sentences planted with care can wait silently for the moment a small cue calls them back.
  • You never know when your smallest true words become the ones someone hears.

We are systematically educated to believe that transformative words belong to the great names. Plato. Socrates. Shakespeare or Rumi (who, incidentally, is often reported to be the best-selling poet in the United States, a fact that surprises everyone who assumes the answer is Shakespeare). We collect their sentences, frame them, tattoo them, and post them, trusting that wisdom this old and this polished must be what changes lives.

Almost three decades as a psychotherapist taught me something different. The words that actually save people are small. They are not addressed to humanity. They are addressed, by accident and with perfect timing, to one person. Two stories—from two countries, two cultures, two lives that never touched—taught me this better than any philosophy could. (Details have been altered to protect privacy; the first story is shared with its subject's blessing.)

Mama

He was 18 when we met, and his grief was among the most severe I have encountered. His mother had died when he was 11, and he had never recovered. Across four long sessions, he repeatedly denied any thought of harming himself. At the end of our last one, I asked him whether he believed his mother was still with him. Everywhere, he said. He talked with her constantly in his mind. Then think of this, I said: if she is everywhere with you, imagine how much it would hurt her to watch her son hurt.

One morning, some time later, he made a quiet, careful plan to end his life, set his room in order, and left to carry it out—the only way, in his mind, to be reunited with her. At the train station, a girl of perhaps 3 played beside her mother. She fell, hurt her knee, and cried out: "Mama, mama." The same word. The same tone he had once used, calling for his own mother.

And with that, my sentence came back to him: If she is everywhere with you, how much would it hurt her to see you hurt? He stood on the platform for a long moment. Then he took the next train home.

That was 25 years ago. Today he is a doctor of psychology who specializes in helping young people with major trauma. Sometimes I call him for advice. By his own account—and I believe him without hesitation—he has helped several hundred young people take the next train back home.

Home

She was a successful finance executive who had survived years of domestic violence from a partner lost to alcohol and other substances, followed by a separation that stretched across three years. She carried the diagnoses that such years produce—depression, PTSD, anxiety—and a pharmacy of medications she had tried.

One evening she offered a junior colleague a ride. Delighted by her elegant car, he was asked to enter his address into the navigation system. He pressed the key, and at the top of the screen was one word: Home. He asked, innocently: "Where is your home?"

She froze. What she wanted to say was: I have no home. There is no "home" for me. She held back her tears, pretended not to hear, delivered him, drove away, stopped the car, and wept. Then she asked herself the question the navigation screen had asked her: Do I have a home?

She drove to her parents' house that night. She took six months of unpaid leave. We met every week. Ten weeks later, she drove back to her own house—and for the first time in years, it was her home.

Why Small Words Reach Us When Famous Ones Cannot

Psychology offers a clue to what happened on that platform and in that car. Memory research shows that what we retrieve depends profoundly on the cues around us: information returns when something in the present matches the way it was originally encoded (Tulving and Thomson, 1973). A quotation from Plato matches nothing in particular. But Mama, in a child's frightened voice, matched everything—his oldest attachment, his deepest loss, and, crucially, the sentence a therapist had once tied to that very bond. The little girl did not quote anyone. She unlocked something.

Small words also work because they are ours. Our autobiographical memory is organized around the self—around the people, places, and words that define who we are (Conway and Pleydell-Pearce, 2000). Home is not a concept to a survivor of domestic violence; it is a wound with an address. When an innocent question touched that word, it did what no prescription had done: it made the loss undeniable—and the repair imaginable.

And notice what neither speaker knew. The girl was not trying to save anyone. The colleague was making small talk. The most powerful words in these two lives were spoken by people who never learned what they had done. Famous words are addressed to everyone and therefore to no one. Small words arrive addressed to you.

What This Asks of Us

You cannot schedule a train-station moment. But you can do three things. Say the small true thing—the plain sentence, the honest question—because you will never know which of your words is waiting to become someone's cue. If you are a therapist, a parent, a teacher, or a friend, plant sentences with care; they can lie dormant for months and wake at exactly the right moment, carried back by a child's cry or a word on a screen. And listen for your own small words—the ones that make you freeze, the ones you pretend not to hear. They usually point at the very thing that needs your attention.

A boy was brought home by a toddler's cry. A woman was brought home by a navigation screen—no marble statues, no collected works, no framed quotations.

No quote from Plato. The small words of a small girl.

item.title: Transcending Insulated Narcissism in the Age of Self-Help
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Transcending Insulated Narcissism in the Age of Self-Help

Personal Perspective: Internet wisdom oversimplifies real human experience.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Many Internet posts and some self-help articles use negative labels as if they were explanations.
  • On the Internet, negative judgments and inflammatory attributions masquerade as facts.
  • Most posts are written to validate feelings and gratify the ego, rather than search for truth.
  • It can seem like narcissism, but our selfie-culture is more a product of immature thinking than pathology.

An abundance of relationship books, articles, and blogs inadvertently contributes to monocular vision—in the name of validation. It thereby impairs the ability to see other perspectives alongside our own.

Here are signs that you read too much self-help and too many Internet posts:

  • Using labels like gaslighting, narcissist, microaggressions in disagreements
  • Confusing judgments with feelings
  • Confusing opinions with scientific findings
  • Accepting citations as truth, without looking up the studies and noting their limitations

It’s hard these days to find an Internet post, or self-help article, or family dispute, much less a political speech, which does not pretend that labels are explanations and opinions are facts. In social and political discourse, all sides are likely to use identical or similar labels to devalue each other.

Labels are terrible explanations. They omit more information than they describe, and obscure more than they illuminate. All labels oversimplify. Sadly, words that highlight serious social issues, such as racist and misogynist, are now widely used as slurs. We use labels because, as Carl Jung put it, "Thinking is hard, that's why people judge." It’s extremely hard to know something, but extremely easy to think we know.

The Cult of “I Feel”

Perhaps recognizing that negative attributions make things worse, not to mention reinforce narcissistic tendencies, common relationship advice tries to hide negative judgments by expressing them as feelings. For example:

“I feel offended, disrespected, judged, dismissed, unheard….”

These are not feelings. They’re judgments, if not accusations, about other people’s attitudes or behavior, which is why they usually elicit counter judgments and accusations. Feelings are guilt, shame, sadness, interest, enjoyment, surprise. Expressing feelings can bring us closer together; negative judgments masquerading as feelings drive us further apart. Feelings are always real and valid, even when the perceptions, assumptions, and judgments that underlie them are inaccurate, false, or unrealistic. For emotional growth, validate feelings but question what underlies them.

The Cult of Opinion

Opinions expressed in the media (particularly on the Internet) are not facts. They may include interpretations of facts, but even then, they’re embedded with personal biases and supported by confirmation bias. Opinions are typically short-hand explanations of complex issues. Those who express them, when they bother to give reasons, never give alternative plausible explanations, of which there are almost always several. We’re more likely to accept the opinions of those who agree with our biases in comparison with those who present compelling evidence.

Appeals to Authority

It’s become fashionable for Internet posts to cite psychological studies as references, giving the false impression that they're on a par with peer-reviewed professional journals. Many years ago, I sat on a peer-review committee of a professional publication. To this day, I remain shocked by the number of submissions citing studies that did not support, and sometimes contradicted, the points in their content. I would have thought they’d be more careful, knowing they were going to be reviewed. I now believe this faulty scholarship was a product of confirmation bias rather than sloppiness, narcissism, or dishonesty.

The most egregious examples of misleading citations do not occur in psychological research literature. For example, several articles published by prestigious medical journals purported that OxyContin was non-addictive. The “study” they cited turned out to be a letter to the editor, quoted out of context, about terminally ill patients who were too sick to exhibit signs of addiction.

Alas, points made in popular literature far surpass professional submissions in misinterpreting or misrepresenting psychological research findings. Even when authors correctly cite studies, they rarely give the published limitations of the studies they cite, few of which are generalizable and replicated.

Toddlers Are So Cute

The self-obsession of toddlers, whose favorite words are Mine and No, is adorable. Not so cute are adults who think like toddlers, preoccupied with splitting and all-or-nothing judgments. Although it can seem like narcissism, the selfie-culture we live in is more a product of immature thinking, of wanting attention by seeming to be smart, morally attractive, or interesting.

If you want to be interesting, be interested. Novelty stimulates interest, but that’s short-lived and superficial. Interest is sustained by depth, which you can find online if you persevere. Clickbaiting appeals to the autopilot toddler brain; depth of thinking occurs in the reflective adult brain.

We become adults when being right is more important than sounding confident, being protective is more important than being protected, offering compassion is more important than receiving it, and loving is more important than being loved.

item.title: What Is Happiness, and Can It Be Attained in Therapy?
item.description:
Therapy

What Is Happiness, and Can It Be Attained in Therapy?

Is happiness something patients can realistically expect to gain from therapy?

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Can psychotherapy patients expect happiness as a consequence of therapy?
  • Releasing unrealistic expectations about life increases happiness and reduces suffering.
  • Mindfully embracing the present moment, instead of resisting reality, fosters contentment.

Is happiness something patients can expect as a realistic consequence of therapy? What does the quintessential clinical wisdom of psychotherapy say about happiness and how to attain it? This is a complex question we initially addressed in Part 1 of this series and continue to consider here.

Existentialism, Meaning, and Meaninglessness

The emphasis in existential therapy on the innate human need for a sense of significance, meaning, and purpose speaks volumes to what truly supports happiness. Suffering without meaning, notes existential psychiatrist and psychotherapist Viktor Frankl (1985), tends to lead to despair. But if life's suffering can be imbued with meaning, despair can potentially be transformed to joy, or perhaps contentment or fulfillment, something akin to so-called happiness. This is why existentialist author Albert Camus (1955) concludes that the tragic Greek figure Sisyphus, sentenced by the gods to eternally roll an enormous stone up a steep hill only to have it roll right back down at the end of each day for the crime of attempting to evade death, must be imagined as being happy. Despite his incessant daily suffering and unendingly tedious task, he has his raison d'etre, his reason for being, his assigned purpose in life, which he accepts rather than resists.

This act of consciously choosing even that fate which, by definition, we cannot control in life is an attitude referred to by another existentially oriented psychotherapist, Otto Rank (1936), as "the willing affirmation of the must." In this sense, we are all a little like Sisyphus: It is only when we are ready and willing to accept and embrace our existential fate—be it our birth, parents, family, genetics, culture, talents, limitations, mortality and so many other of life's non-negotiable givens we did not choose and, thus, bear no personal responsibility for—rather than furiously fighting futilely against it, that we too can attain the contentment, satisfaction, and presumed happiness, contentment, and satisfaction of Sisyphus.

Psychoanalysis and Buddhism

Happiness, held Freud, is all relative, viewing greater (though not total) freedom from neurotic suffering as perhaps the most that psychotherapy can offer. (See Part 1.) Life consists of at least some unavoidable suffering, tragedy, loss, sadness, illness, and, therefore, unhappiness. According to Freud, we are constitutionally, both psychologically and physiologically, creatures more inclined to unhappiness than happiness. We must not realistically expect happiness to be our normal state of mind. But this was certainly no completely new existential insight proffered by Freud. Siddhartha Gautama, better known as the Buddha, said something quite similar which practitioners of Buddhism have known for thousands of years: Life is suffering. Suffering causes unhappiness. The source of this suffering is excessive attachment, desire, or dukkha. Happiness requires relinquishing these illusory attachments, addictions, and desires.

CBT, REBT, and Irrational Beliefs

Psychologist Albert Ellis, considered the grandfather of CBT, started his career as a Freudian psychoanalyst; he eventually applied his lifelong fascination with classical philosophy, including Buddhism, to his own cognitively focused form of psychotherapy he referred to as rational emotive behavior therapy (REBT). For Ellis, as for the Buddha, the root of unhappiness has to do with wanting and insisting the world meet our often unrealistic or irrational expectations. The more we can release these irrational expectations or beliefs about existence, people, ourselves, and replace them with more realistic and rational ones, the happier we become—less frustrated, disappointed, resentful, angry, and miserable. But how can this be clinically accomplished?

In therapy, Ellis actively engaged in aggressive "disputation" of these unrealistic expectations or illusions regarding the way life "should" be, "ought" to be, or "must" be, directly challenging the patient or client to reconsider the veracity of these often deeply and dearly held but self-defeating convictions. For example, to the patient's grievance about being treated unfairly by life, Ellis might counter: "Who told you that life is fair?" Thus launching into a psychoeducational and philosophical conversation regarding the need to alter our irrational or unrealistic beliefs and attitudes about how life should be. As with Aaron Beck's cognitive behavioral therapy, which evolved directly from REBT, the point is that the way we think about things can influence how we feel and behave, for better or worse. The goal of REBT is not to eliminate but to transform these irrational or distorted beliefs and demands on reality into more rational, realistic preferences. Such unrealistic or irrational expectations set us up for frequent frustration, anger, rage, and, over time, embitterment, resentment, and unhappiness because reality repeatedly fails to meet our needs. Thus, for example, the irrational belief that "people should always be good" or "life must always be fair," in REBT becomes modified to "I would prefer life to be that way, but I can accept that sometimes (or maybe even most of the time) it may not be." We make ourselves miserable by clinging to unrealistic expectations but can make ourselves happier by consciously relinquishing them.

Being Fully Present and Mindful in the Moment

Ultimately, one's happiness is not necessarily determined by whether life is fair or not, tedious or not, painful or not, whether one has a significant other right now or not, whether one is wealthy or not, receives the grade desired in some class, nor even whether one has serious problems with their physical or mental health. Armed with this way of thinking, this helpful clinical wisdom (see my prior post), one is no longer rigidly attached to life always being a certain desired way but rather goes more with the flow, accepting and embracing rather than resisting and rejecting existential reality as it is right here and now.

Whatever that reality may be in this ephemeral yet eternal moment, which changes constantly like water in a raging river. To cite the pre-Socratic Greek philosopher Heraclitus, "No man ever steps in the same river twice, for it's not the same river and he's not the same man." The secret here is that whatever our situation or circumstance, we can learn to choose to stay in the present, to willfully direct our consciousness only to what is happening right now—not yesterday or tomorrow—and to focus on fully experiencing and appreciating the present moment and what it offers, exactly as it is, as opposed to how we wish it to be. Be it pleasurable or painful, joyful or sorrowful. If we can learn to discipline ourselves and take this virtual meditative approach to existence, we will have, at least to some extent, transcended the vagaries and vicissitudes of existence that hamper happiness and discovered how to live more fully in the here and now.

item.title: Projective Identification: Being Force-Fed Feelings
item.description:
Projection

Projective Identification: Being Force-Fed Feelings

The injustice of being made to swallow shame that is not yours.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Projective identification goes beyond projection: the feeling enters your emotional system.
  • The projector is usually not acting with conscious intent but evacuating pain they cannot hold.
  • Projective identification can be harder to detect than gaslighting.

Most people have heard of projection, and most people, once they understand the concept, can spot it without too much difficulty. Projective identification is qualitatively different and far harder to catch.

In projective identification, a person who cannot tolerate something in themselves—shame, fear of vulnerability, a sense of their own inadequacy—unconsciously behaves in ways that induce that very feeling in you. The feeling does not arrive as an accusation you can examine and reject. By the time you notice it, it feels like it has always originated from you.

What gets deposited in projective identification is not simply a transient feeling of anxiety, shame, or self-doubt, but the other person's entire relationship with the unacceptable parts of themselves. Their experience of themselves as inadequate, or as failing, the whole embodied experience of what it was like to carry those heavy, soul-piercing wounds gets into your system.

How It Might Feel

You leave a conversation with a close friend and find yourself flooded with self-disgust. Nothing was said directly, no accusation was made, but you walk to your car feeling like there is something fundamentally wrong with you. You replay the conversation looking for what you did, and you cannot find it, but the feeling is so strong that you assume you must be missing something. Or you spend an afternoon with a family member who seems perfectly pleasant throughout, and by evening you are gripped by an anxiety so intense it feels physical. You did not feel this way before you saw them. You do not normally feel this way.

When one person's unprocessed self-rejection finds lodging in another, the deposited material is often organised around shame, intense self-doubt, and despair. You may find yourself revisiting the interaction obsessively, ruminating over what you did wrong. You may lose your footing entirely, sliding from a manageable and ordinary degree of self-doubt into a full collapse of your sense of who you are.

And eerily, you may forget to be angry. There may be a flicker of resentment, but it is thin, and it is overridden almost immediately by self-doubt. You are hardly seeing what happened as something done to you. Rather, you are only busy asking what is wrong with you. The absence of outward-directed anger is often a part of the mechanism itself.

When projective identification happens in an intimate relationship, it often hides behind fixed roles and seemingly affectionate habits that appear natural to everyone involved. Consider a partner who cannot tolerate their own vulnerability. They cannot bear the feeling of being small, or frightened, or needy, because somewhere in their childhood or history, those feelings were met with contempt or abandonment. So through projective identification, they try to evacuate the unbearable feelings of being vulnerable. They may do this through a hundred small, daily acts that are easy to miss. Something like a teasing nickname, a habit of framing their partner's concerns as overreactions, a way of positioning themselves as the one who copes while their partner is the one who struggles. None of these acts, taken individually, looks like anything. Taken together, over months and years, they produce a partner who feels increasingly convinced that they are the fragile one in the relationship. The mechanism makes the recipient look like the source. Projective identification is in some ways harder to detect than gaslighting.

What they are doing to you is awful, and it is often cruel and unjust in its effects, but it is hardly intentional or malicious. The projector is likely a victim of psychological harm or deprivation themselves. Someone who often resorts to pathological projective identification has so little mental capacity that whenever they hit something within themselves that they cannot hold, be it self-disgust, shame, a sense of their own inadequacy, they need to get rid of it to just get through the next day. In other words, they are absolutely desperate, and projective identification might have been the only tool available to them at the time.

The Injustice of It

The loneliest part of this process is that the other person will almost certainly never acknowledge what happened. The injustice of that may tempt you toward actions that feel nothing but fair but actually make things worse. Even when what you are calling out is exactly what is happening, when it is directed at someone who does not have the emotional capacity to truly listen it will likely backfire. It may result in more gaslighting, more episodes of being told that you are the problem, the sensitive one, the "too much" one, the toxic one. Remember, the reason the whole thing happened was that they were desperately trying to protect themselves from their own unbearable material.

You will probably not receive an apology or a moment of mutual understanding. The grief of that may have to be digested in another way, and the closure created by alternative rituals within your own control. Holding your anger and resentment without acting on them, without letting the urgency of the injustice push you into something that ultimately harms you further, is perhaps the hardest part of the whole process.

What to Do With Projective Identification

There is no clean protocol for how to deal with pathological projective identification, as each dynamic is uniquely different and comes with its own nuances. But as a general rule, you can practise getting better and better at recognising it and coping with it. Each time the shame or the self-doubt resurfaces, you locate it in your body, and you remind yourself that it is not yours, at least not entirely. You do not need to confront the person or reach any particular conclusion about their character, or feel a clean, resolved anger at them. You only need to keep reminding yourself that something has happened and what you feel is not pointing to the whole truth about who you are. Eventually, the grip will get weaker, and it will leave your system faster.

Projective identification takes a complex, full, multidimensional person and flattens them into a single description: too much, too needy, too difficult, too broken. To recover, you must, summoning all the mental strength you have, remember that you are more than the version of you that the mechanism produced.

Your resilience will eventually come back, and when your intact sense of self does return, having survived a horrid episode of projective identification with all the resentment and betrayal that came with it, you may find that you have come back changed. You are somehow toughened by the episode. You become less naive, more alert, more able to feel the early weight of someone else's material before it settles into your bones. You become a little more, though not entirely, immune to projective identification.

item.title: The Social Tax of Autism
item.description:
Autism

The Social Tax of Autism

Social skills and autism: How social skills can impact every aspect of life.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Autistic adults are often judged negatively within seconds, despite trying to fit in.
  • Social acceptance shapes opportunity, making everyday life harder for many autistic adults.
  • The social systems that shape daily life often exclude autistic adults before they can belong.

Our modern society is dominated by conformity and social structures. Businesses, homeowners associations, schools, churches, nonprofit organizations, and civic groups shape nearly every aspect of modern life. They influence whether we maintain employment, pay our bills, find support when we need it, and successfully navigate an increasingly complex world.

One example of this influence is the homeowners association. In many communities, it is nearly impossible to purchase a home or condominium without joining an HOA that exercises significant control over daily life. A recent Jacksonville case became national news after a younger homeowner inherited her father's house in a 55+ community. According to news reports, neighbors were openly divided, with some publicly stating, "She should move." The homeowner reported years of pressure, revoked privileges, and legal action while attempting to remain in her late father's home. In another case, a California homeowner described what he believed was a "personal vendetta" after receiving repeated violation notices while neighbors with similar issues were left alone. The HOA denied those allegations and stated that it was enforcing its rules consistently.

The Influence of Social Groups

HOAs are only one example of how our lives are shaped by social groups. Parent-teacher organizations, churches, schools, volunteer organizations, and civic groups all influence opportunities, relationships, and the communities in which we live.

These social systems can be overwhelming for anyone. For autistic adults, however, they present a unique challenge because autism fundamentally affects social communication. In a society where success often depends on navigating unwritten social rules, the consequences can be profound.

Research shows that neurotypical adults often form negative first impressions of autistic people, even when autistic individuals are actively trying to fit in. Sasson and colleagues (2017) found that neurotypical participants were less willing to interact socially with autistic adults after only a few seconds of exposure. More recently, a 2025 meta-analysis synthesizing 21 studies and 221 effect sizes concluded that autistic people consistently receive less favorable first impressions than non-autistic people across nearly every presentation format except written transcripts. The authors concluded that these differences are driven largely by differences in nonverbal communication rather than by the content of what autistic people say.

Trying to Succeed in a Conformity-Focused World

That finding should force us to ask an uncomfortable question: How are autistic adults expected to succeed in a world where social acceptance and social conformity influence nearly every aspect of adult life?

Much of our attention is focused on autistic children. We teach them to blend in, make eye contact, suppress stimming, and act as "normally" as possible. Yet the research suggests that even autistic adults who become highly skilled at masking are often still perceived as awkward, off-putting, or difficult by neurotypical observers. If fitting in remains elusive despite tremendous effort, then maintaining employment, finding housing, participating in community organizations, and accessing support become far more difficult than many people realize.

One autistic adult on Reddit captured this experience with heartbreaking simplicity:

"Am I just doomed to be alone forever unless I regain my ability to fake my entire existence?"

As an autistic adult, I feel that question in my bones.

The truth is that even when I am trying to fake my entire existence, I often fail to meet neurotypical expectations. My own HOA is largely shaped by neurotypical voices who value things I don’t even understand and have difficulty conforming to because they don’t make sense to me. I volunteer at neighborhood events, attend meetings, and genuinely try to be friendly. Yet we seem to receive an endless stream of complaints over issues that often make little sense to me. We mow our lawn. We address every complaint. Still, the conflict never seems to be about the property itself. It feels rooted in my interactions with neighbors and their discomfort with someone who is profoundly different.

Unfortunately, this has not been limited to my neighborhood. I have experienced similar patterns in workplaces, nonprofit organizations, volunteer groups, and countless community groups I genuinely wanted to be part of. No matter how much I mask, volunteer, or try to help, I eventually find myself becoming disliked and shunned.

Consequences of Social Rejection for Autistic Adults

The cost of this constant social rejection is staggering. Autistic adults experience dramatically elevated rates of unemployment, anxiety, depression, and suicide compared with the general population. Many lose jobs they believed they were performing well in, often after receiving positive evaluations, only to hear vague explanations such as, "You weren't a good fit," "You were disrespectful," or "You made people uncomfortable." The tragedy is that many autistic adults are completely unaware they have violated social expectations because those expectations were never explicitly communicated. Some autistic people's inability to read social cues can make them unaware of the ways they may be upsetting those around them.

Autistic people spend their lives trying to understand neurotypical culture. We study it, rehearse it, imitate it, and often exhaust ourselves trying to belong. Masking and pretending to be normal has been shown to have a profound impact on autistic mental health and suicide rates and it is a daily part of our existence. Maybe it is time to ask neurotypical society to meet us halfway.

The solution cannot be asking autistic people to become better at pretending to be someone else. Instead, we must become more willing to question our own assumptions about likability, professionalism, friendliness, respect and what it means to "fit in." There is extraordinary beauty in human diversity, but that beauty can only flourish when we stop demanding conformity as the price of living in society.

item.title: Partner Violence Is Less Recognized in LGBTQ Relationships
item.description:
Domestic Violence

Why Partner Violence Less Recognized in LGBTQ Relationships

Bias and discrimination make LGBTQ survivors less likely to be supported.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • LGBTQ survivors face unique barriers to leaving abusive relationships.
  • Stigma and discrimination can keep abuse hidden and unreported.
  • Policies that support all survivors would help protect those who are marginalized.

Eric sat quietly for a moment before speaking. "I know everyone thinks the answer is simple," he said. "Just leave. But they don't see what happens after that. They don't see how hard it is to try."

He described how his partner had repeatedly threatened to out both him and their relationship—something Eric feared could cost him his job or even jeopardize the partial custody he shared with his ex-girlfriend over their daughter. Whenever Eric talked about ending the relationship, his partner reminded him of the discrimination they had already faced as a couple: "Who do you think is going to believe a gay man when he says he's being abused?" Other times, he warned Eric that leaving would only reinforce the stereotypes people already held about same-sex relationships.

"I don't even know what's real anymore," Eric told me. "Part of me knows this isn't healthy. The other part wonders if leaving is even possible."

Like many survivors, Eric wasn't staying because he failed to recognize the harm. He was staying because years of coercion, realistic fears about the consequences of leaving, and the limited support available to many LGBTQ survivors had made his escape feel far more dangerous. The isolation and the very real fear of losing his livelihood, his family, and his support system made leaving feel far more dangerous than anyone on the outside could see.

Source: Image created by ChatGPT

LGBTQ Survivors of Abuse Face Additional Barriers to Leaving

Leaving a harmful or abusive relationship is frightening enough to push anyone into a state of worry. But Eric’s reality, like that of many LGBTQ survivors, is different simply because of who they are. My practice specializes in working with LGBTQ individuals and treating abuse and trauma survivors. I often witness the twofold suffering they experience as members of a marginalized community: first the trauma and then the stigma. The self-doubt that abusers instill, compounded with minority stressors, makes it even less likely that LGBTQ victims will come forward about their abuse.

Perpetrators use this stigma and general ignorance about these relationship dynamics against LGBTQ partners. They might tell them that no one will take their claim seriously or threaten to “out” them if they try, as in Eric's case. Some victims may even stay quiet out of fear of tarnishing the reputation of others within the community with anything that would further marginalize them from society.

Abuse in LGBTQ Relationships Is Less Recognized

Many victims are unaware that abuse can even exist within these relationships. Research of non-heterosexual partner dynamics has only recently become a topic of conversation. It wasn't until the CDC's 2010–2012 National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey that the federal government published comprehensive national estimates of intimate partner violence among lesbian, gay, and bisexual adults. The results highlighted rates of abuse that demanded greater attention and more inclusive support services. According to their analysis, lesbians and bisexual men are more likely to encounter violent physical abuse than their heterosexual counterparts.

Yet, despite the greater risk, many domestic violence support networks still have yet to accommodate their resources to LGBTQ victims.

item.title: Teaching Companies to Tell Stories With Data
item.description:
Empathy

Teaching Companies to Tell Stories With Data

Interview with Sienna Jackson on leveraging the arts for greater data impact.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Data works best when it validates lived experience.
  • Stories make information emotionally relevant, which helps turn understanding into action.
  • Impact reports work better when stakeholders are heroes and data maps their progress.
Source: Vitaly Gariev/Unsplash

If you've worked in a company setting, you have likely sat in a room where someone presents a slide deck loaded with charts, numbers, and bullet points. The presenter seems prepared, and everyone nods politely. But do you really remember what is shared, and do you really care about the data or act on it? Often, that answer is no.

But picture another scenario, where that same data is introduced through the life of one person, such as someone with an obstacle, an underdog position, a turning point, and a victorious outcome. Suddenly, those same dry numbers have a human pulse. You find yourself remembering, caring about, and acting on what you learned.

The difference between those two scenarios is captured and demystified in this interview. Drawing from her work helping others to tell stories with data, Sienna Jackson shows us what organizations can learn from entertainment, and how teaching these arts can make complex or uncomfortable data easier for audiences to face. Jackson's answers follow each question below.

Jenny Grant Rankin (JGR): Why is storytelling such a powerful driver of action, and what have you discovered about why facts alone rarely move people?

Sienna Jackson (SJ): Facts provide the framework for understanding, but they rarely provide the impulse for movement. As a strategist who operates at the intersection of “Cause, Capital and Culture,” I have seen that data alone is often treated as abstract. Humans are biologically wired to process information through narrative; when we hear a story, our brains synchronize with the storyteller, bypassing intellectual defenses and activating the empathic centers of the brain.

Facts appeal to the analytical mind, which is prone to skepticism and fatigue—especially in today's information-dense environment. Not to mention that “information” does not necessarily translate to “knowledge” in an era of aggressive disinformation and generative AI slop. Conversely, stories establish emotional relevance, which is the primary catalyst for decision-making.

Impact measurement has taught me that the most effective data sets are those that provide the evidence for a narrative that has already won the audience's heart. It is better to move people by using data to validate their lived experience rather than asking them to calculate their empathy.

JGR: You've worked on films like Fruitvale Station, The Imitation Game, and Lion—stories that crossed cultural lines and shifted public consciousness. What does entertainment get right about storytelling that organizations and educators often get wrong?

SJ: The film industry inherently understands that the “protagonist” is more important than the “program.” I’ve seen firsthand how entertainment prioritizes human vulnerability—the journey, the conflict, and the transformation—over the abstract concepts of the issue itself, which serve as background to the narrative.

Organizations and educators often get it wrong by prioritizing the output or the process. They lead with the what—the policy, the curriculum, or the technical data—before establishing the who or why. Entertainment succeeds because it uses suspension of disbelief to make the audience identify with someone unlike themselves. Organizations often treat their audience as recipients of information, whereas successful storytelling treats them as witnesses to a life.

When nonprofit organizations learn to frame their impact reports, for example, as a human journey—where the stakeholders are the heroes and the data is simply the map of their progress—they stop being viewed as recipients of charity and start being viewed as collaborators and catalysts for change.

JGR: How can culture and the arts serve as a bridge, connecting communities, shaping social norms, and making complex or uncomfortable truths more accessible?

SJ: Culture and the arts act as a neutral ground where the cost of entry is empathy rather than expertise. By building initiatives bridging the arts and activism, I have seen how creative spaces allow people to navigate complex social realities—such as systemic inequality or historical trauma—without feeling overwhelmed by technical jargon or defensiveness about policy.

Art provides a safe container for uncomfortable truths. It translates the unfamiliar into something human and accessible. When we produce events that convene diverse stakeholder groups or curate soundtracks that evoke a specific emotional resonance for a film, we are creating a cultural bridge that allows the audience to “try on” a new perspective.

Shifting the conversation from a lecture to a creative dialogue makes complex situational and social dynamics accessible and, more importantly, shared. This shared experience is what eventually shifts social norms; you cannot legislate empathy, but you can cultivate it through cultural connection.

item.title: Not All People With BPD Are the Same—Why Is Their Treatment?
item.description:
Personality

Not All People With BPD Are the Same—Why Is Their Treatment?

Why people with the same diagnosis may need very different interventions.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • People with the same BPD diagnosis can have symptoms driven by different processes.
  • Current evidence-based BPD treatments target different mechanisms of change.
  • Matching treatment to the person may improve outcomes and shorten recovery.

A few years ago, I took on two new clients within a few weeks of each other. I remember being struck by how similar they were. Both were diagnosed with borderline personality disorder (BPD) and both struggled with alcohol use and over-spending.

But as we started talking about what happened in the moments before they used, it became clear they weren't actually struggling with the same problem at all.

One patient reached for alcohol or her credit card whenever her negative emotions became overwhelming. Drinking and shopping offered temporary relief from shame, sadness, and anxiety. My other patient described these behaviors as something that happened automatically whenever the opportunity presented itself. Instead of numbing emotional pain, she was saying yes to whatever felt exciting in the moment.

Seeing these patients side-by-side changed the way I think about treating BPD. If two people can arrive at the diagnosis—and even the same symptoms (risky substance use and reckless spending)—through different psychological pathways, why would we assume they need exactly the same intervention?

One Diagnosis, Many Pathways

One of the biggest misconceptions about mental health conditions is that all people with the same disorder present the same way. In reality, many diagnoses (e.g., depression, post-traumatic stress disorder) are remarkably heterogeneous. This is particularly true for BPD. There are 256 different combinations of the (5 of 9) DSM criteria that can result in receiving the diagnosis. Moreover, two people can share a BPD diagnosis with only one symptom in common.

For some people, BPD symptoms are primarily driven by intense negative emotions. Others struggle most with difficulties trusting others, whereas are highly impulsive. Many people with this condition experience several of these difficulties, but the degree to which each contributes to their suffering varies considerably.

One-Size-Fits-All Treatment

We have several treatments for BPD that have accumulated strong scientific support. In dialectical behavior therapy (DBT), BPD is considered to fundamentally be a disorder of emotion dysregulation. The treatment focuses on helping people tolerate distress and respond to intense emotions more effectively.

By contrast, in mentalization-based treatment (MBT) and transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP), the emphasis is on improving how people interpret and respond to relationships, including the expectations they bring into interactions with others.

Despite targeting different psychological processes, these treatments produce similar outcomes when compared head-to-head. In general, DBT, MBT, and TFP all lead to meaningful improvement for many patients after about a year of twice-weekly therapy.

At the same time, many patients don't respond to these treatments. Because they are one-size-fits-all, it’s possible that non-responders received an intervention that didn’t match the process actually driving their symptoms.

The Behavior Isn't Always the Mechanism

Consider my two patients again.

An emotion-focused intervention like DBT would be a great fit for the client who was drinking and shopping to escape emotional pain.

But for the patient who engaged in reckless behavior because she craved stimulation and excitement, that same intervention might miss the mark.

Even though their behaviors were the same, the processes driving them were not.

The same principle applies across many symptoms of BPD. People with this condition may have frequent interpersonal conflicts because they tend to have big emotional reactions and would be a good fit for DBT. Or, they might have difficulties in relationships because they’re suspicious of others’ motives and would respond better to one of the relational treatments (TFP, MBT).

Matching Treatment to the Person

BPD Compass is a new treatment approach for people with BPD that was explicitly designed for personalized treatment plans. Rather than assuming every person with BPD should receive the same intervention, Compass begins by identifying the psychological processes most responsible for maintaining that individual's symptoms.

The treatment starts with an assessment to determine which psychological processes are driving your symptoms. Then, clients work through the modules that are most relevant to them.

In clinical trials, BPD Compass led to significant reductions in BPD symptoms. And, because the psychological processes targeted are also relevant to other disorders, the treatment also improved symptoms of depression, anxiety, eating disorders, and substance use disorders.

Additionally, since BPD Compass is personalized and provides the most relevant skills first, it can be delivered in 18 weeks—a much shorter duration than existing treatments.

Looking Beyond the Diagnosis

A diagnosis tells us what problems someone is experiencing. It doesn't necessarily tell us why those problems persist.

As our understanding of BPD continues to evolve, I believe the future of treatment lies not in discovering one therapy that's better than all the others, but in becoming better at matching evidence-based interventions to the people who are most likely to benefit from them.

After all, if not all people with BPD look the same, there's little reason to expect they should all need exactly the same treatment.

item.title: Aging Well at Any Age
item.description:
Aging

Aging Well at Any Age

Embracing the opportunity to thrive at every stage of life.

Posted August 2, 2026

Key points
  • Cultivate a growth mindset and reframe common age-related thoughts.
  • Stay curious. Our brains benefit from lifelong learning.
  • Invest in relationships. Healthy relationships are strong predictors of our emotional well-being.
  • Live with purpose. Purpose gives us direction and motivation.

For many, aging is thought of in what we lose—our youth, physical stamina, or familiar routines. As a psychologist and someone who recently celebrated a milestone birthday, this perspective tells only part of the story. While aging inevitably brings change, it also offers remarkable opportunities for growth, resilience, and deeper fulfillment. In a nutshell, aging is not only about growing older, but also about continuing to grow.

One of the greatest misconceptions about aging is that personal growth has an expiration date. But in fact, our capacity to learn, develop meaningful relationships, discover new interests, and contribute to the world and others around us can continue, if we choose, throughout our lives. Research consistently shows that healthy aging is influenced by more than genetics. The choices we make every day—physically, emotionally, socially, and mentally—play a significant role in our well-being. In fact, in my practice, I often remind clients that cultivating a growth mindset can greatly shape one’s experience and attitude towards aging.

The psychologist Carol Dweck introduced the concept of a growth mindset to describe the belief that our qualities are not fixed but can be strengthened through effort, learning, and experience. While much of the research has focused on children and education, the principles are equally relevant later in life. The brain remains capable of forming new neural connections, adapting to challenges, and learning throughout life.

A growth mindset encourages us to reframe common age-related thoughts:

  • ﻿﻿Fixed mindset: "I'm too old to start exercising."
    Growth mindset: "My body can become stronger at any age."
  • ﻿﻿Fixed mindset: "My memory isn't what it used to be."
    Growth mindset: " I can support my brain through learning, exercise, sleep, and healthy habits."
  • Fixed mindset: "It's too late to make new friends."
    Growth mindset: "Meaningful relationships can develop at any age.”

The reality is, aging is a privilege, and not everyone gets the chance to experience it. And how we choose to approach and view aging can make our later years some of the happiest of our lives. Below are a few recommendations for cultivating a growth mindset so you can thrive at every stage of life:

  1. Stay physically active. It's no surprise that movement supports our physical health, but movement also greatly affects our emotional well-being. Exercise is just as effective for treating depression and anxiety as antidepressants. It's important to find physical activities you enjoy since we're more likely to be consistent when we like them.
  2. Keep your mind engaged. Stay curious. Read, learn a new skill, explore a hobby, or challenge yourself intellectually. I have stayed curious by attending drawing classes and reading classic novels I had not had the time to read previously. Lifelong learning keeps us curious and connected to the world around us.
  3. Invest in relationships. Healthy relationships are among the strongest predictors of emotional well-being. Prioritize making the time to spend with friends, family, and your community. Meaningful relationships and connections are essential for everyone regardless of age. My volunteer work at a community center helps those in need in my community, and I have also made new friendships with other like-minded people.
  4. Find your purpose. Having a reason to get up each morning, whether it’s for work, volunteering, mentoring, creative pursuits, or caring for loved ones, supports our mental and emotional health. Purpose shapes our lives by giving it direction and meaning. Having a purpose also provides value to every stage of life.
